author: Amir Guterman
body:
Scaffolds teamme onto itself: six specialists derived from the repo's real
layer boundaries, a tailored /intake command, and the five hook scripts copied
verbatim from the templates they ship.

The hook copies under .claude/hooks/ are byte-identical to
plugins/teamme/templates/hooks/ at install time and nothing keeps them that
way, so CLAUDE.md and the team README both record that the template is the
source of truth.

Verified with ./scripts/validate.sh plus an in-project pipe test of every hook
phase: idle allows, grounding denies, .claude/ and out-of-project paths are
exempt, approved allows, malformed and stale state allow, and Stop fires once.

author: Amir Guterman
body:
Adds an MCP server, a preflight check and a team-doctor command, so a broken
install reports itself instead of looking healthy. Because every hook fails
open by design, a machine without python3 previously produced an install
indistinguishable from a working one. The server cannot fix that - it makes
it visible: the process fails to start and the harness says so in /mcp, with
no teamme code having run.

teamme_worklog and teamme_intake_phase refuse until teamme_install has run,
naming it in the refusal. preflight.py distinguishes three states that were
previously identical: not-installed, installed-not-live, and live, the last
proven by a SessionStart heartbeat.

Renames build-agent-team to init-team as a clean break, with no alias.

Also fixes three bugs found while building this: the prompt router told every
project to read an ARCHITECTURE.md it does not have, the passthrough regex
never matched the plugin-prefixed command form, and the intake flow's terminal
dispositions returned without releasing the phase lock, leaving a repository
write-locked until the one-hour timeout.

validate.sh gains 206 lines covering all of it, each assertion observed
failing before passing. The prompts remain unproven beyond frontmatter
parsing; there is still no eval suite.

author: Amir Guterman
body:
Three defects in the durable ledger, all found by running the agent team in
parallel rather than by reading the code.

Concurrent writes silently dropped each other: load, mutate and save with no
mutual exclusion lost 3 of 24 notes under measurement. Writes are now atomic
and guarded by a lockfile that expires on a crash and, if it cannot be taken,
proceeds unlocked rather than refusing to record - a ledger that declines to
write is worse than a rare lost note.

The Stop reminder stamped itself against `updated`, which every mutation
touched, so recording progress re-armed it. One of the three remedies the hook
itself suggests therefore guaranteed another interruption. It now stamps
against a separate `status_changed`, so only a real status transition re-arms
it and a note answers it.

Async dispatch had no representation: `active` nagged every turn and `blocked`
told the user they owed an input they did not owe. Adds a `dispatched` status
for work in flight with another agent.

Also adds /teamme:queue, which parks a request in one line without grounding
it, and teaches /intake to test for a deferral signal before the phase check
rather than after.

Fixes the router injecting its reminder for an empty prompt, and a heartbeat
that could hang forever on an un-redirected stdin - on a pty it blocked past
three seconds and now exits in well under one.

validate.sh gains 82 lines covering all of it, each assertion observed failing
before passing. The prompts remain unproven beyond frontmatter parsing.

author: Amir Guterman
body:
Preflight decided whether teamme was installed by counting hook scripts
against REQUIRED_HOOKS. That tuple grows every release, so adding preflight.py
to it meant a complete, working install from an older release scored five of
six and was reported as never installed - then told to run the installer,
which re-runs the questionnaire and regenerates the roster over a team that
already works. Reproduced against a real project carrying the previous
release's scaffolding. It would have met every existing user on upgrade.

Existence is now evidence-based: a settings.json hooks block naming one of
teamme's own scripts, or a generated intake.md. Neither probe changes when a
release adds a hook script, so the failure cannot recur the next time one is
added. A missing hook script became a repair condition instead, under a fourth
state - installed-outdated - whose remediation is never the installer.

An outdated install halts /intake until it is repaired, because the exit code
follows the individual checks rather than the state. That is intended and is
now documented where an upgrading user meets it rather than left to be
discovered.

/queue no longer claims a project is uninstalled when all it knows is that the
work log did not answer; it points at team-doctor, which can actually tell.

validate.sh gains the regression test that matters: a synthetic install from
the previous release must report installed-outdated and must never be told to
run the installer. It was watched failing by restoring the old definition. The
evidence probe is also asserted not to fire on a stranger's repository.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>
subject: Stop preflight calling every existing install uninstalled

author: Amir Guterman
body:
Preflight checked only that each hook script existed. A project carrying
scripts from an older release could be repaired, report live, and still run
the old ones - including the router that told every project to read an
ARCHITECTURE.md it does not have. The installer already compared content and
refused to overwrite a differing file; the health check did not, so the two
disagreed about what a complete install is.

They now share one comparison. Missing and differing are reported separately,
with separate fixes: a hook that merely differs is left alone by a plain
repair, because the difference may be a deliberate local edit, and replacing
it takes force=true.

Freshness is only checked where the plugin's templates can be found, which is
the tools that run inside the plugin. Inside a project the check cannot locate
them, degrades to existence-only and passes, saying so. An upgrading user is
therefore halted by a missing hook but not by one that merely differs - stated
in the changelog entry rather than left to be discovered.

Also fixes a combined missing-and-differing fix line slipping past the guard
that keeps the installer's name out of an existing install's advice.

Released as 0.2.1.

subject: Detect a hook that differs from the copy the plugin ships

author: Amir Guterman
body:
Freshness checking only worked where the plugin's templates were already
reachable, which meant the tools running inside the plugin. The copy living in
a project could not find them, degraded to checking that each hook merely
existed, and passed - so an upgrading user was halted by a missing hook but
never by one that had simply fallen behind.

It now resolves them through the harness's own record of what is installed,
as a last resort after the existing sources. The record is read on every
check, never remembered: the plugin cache keeps old versions side by side, so
a path captured while installing would outlive the next upgrade and compare a
stale hook against an equally stale template, then call it current. Every way
the lookup can fail returns to checking existence alone and says the freshness
was not verified, naming the command that can check properly.

How far this reaches depends on how the plugin was installed, which the
changelog now says: installed for every project, the check works everywhere;
installed for one, it works there and degrades elsewhere. The result names
which of the two happened.

One test was passing for the wrong reason. It asserted the degraded path but
left the environment that decides it untouched, so it held only on a machine
whose plugin happens to be installed the way this one is. It now isolates that
environment, and the record lookup gains cases for resolving, for a missing or
unparseable record, and for a recorded path that must be rejected rather than
trusted.

Released as 0.2.2.

author: Amir Guterman
body:
The ledger gains the two-tier design the librarians need - agents the plugin
ships and enables, distinct from the team it generates per project - along
with the indexing they provide, the storage fork between committing that
index with the code or keeping it alongside, and the tensions each raises: a
database file cannot be merged, a gate that blocks belongs on the hook that
is allowed to block, and a refresh that runs every turn has to stay cheap
enough not to be switched off.

Also records that this repository is currently installing its own plugin from
the working tree rather than from the published branch, which makes every
test here exercise something no user receives.

subject: Record the session librarian and what it must not become

author: Amir Guterman
body:
Phase 1 of the librarian layer: a SQLite store, an incremental git
indexer, and three MCP tools. No librarian agents, no hooks and no
freshness gate yet - those are later phases, and the docs say so
rather than describing a layer that does not exist.

The indexer lives in the plugin rather than in templates/hooks/, so
nothing new is copied into a project and nothing joins REQUIRED_HOOKS.
That avoids T23's trap by construction instead of by remembering: a
copied indexer would make every future librarian grow the list that
already once reported working installs as never-installed.

The database is derived and disposable; the append-only jsonl beside
it is the record. A binary file cannot be merged, so two people
indexing different commits would conflict irreconcilably. rebuild()
reconstructs the whole database from the text with no git access at
all - asserted against ground truth read from git itself, not from
the module, after an earlier draft of that assertion was caught
comparing the code with itself and passing a deliberate bug.

Queries are a bounded named set, not arbitrary SQL. At 9-11ms over
52,947 file rows there is no performance argument for raw SQL, and a
query that answers with an unbounded dump recreates the problem the
index exists to solve.

Also stops the MCP server announcing a stale version: it is read live
from plugin.json, degrading to 0.0.0+unknown if the manifest cannot be
read rather than crashing or inventing a number. The literal had
drifted two minor releases, and /mcp showed it.

Measured: a refresh costs ~12ms when current and ~8ms per commit
incrementally, on a 10,393-commit repo; only the one-time cold index
is expensive at ~15s. validate.sh grows from 23 sections to 34, four
of them watched failing first.
